sources.title: Zero is a young number in human history. How do our brains understand it? (2025-01-01)

facts.text: Zero has two different uses: as a placeholder that keeps other digits in their correct positions (so that 2106 is not confused with 216), and as a number in its own right.
The Babylonians wrote numbers on clay tablets in a place-value system based on 60, and for over 1,000 years it had no mark for an empty place; readers relied on context.
By around 400 BC Babylonian scribes put two wedge marks where we would write a zero, but only between digits, never at the end of a number.
Carbon dating of the Bakhshali manuscript, a birch-bark text found in what is now Pakistan, placed some pages in the third or fourth century; it uses a dot as a placeholder.
The Indian mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in 628, the first known text to treat zero as a number in its own right with rules for calculating with it.
Brahmagupta defined zero as the result of subtracting a number from itself, and stated that adding or subtracting zero leaves a number unchanged and that multiplying by zero gives zero.
Brahmagupta also stated that zero divided by zero equals zero, a rule that is wrong by the standards of modern mathematics.
Indian numerals and zero passed to Arab and Islamic scholars; al-Khwarizmi wrote a book describing the Indian place-value numerals 1 to 9 and 0, and Arab traders carried the system west.
Fibonacci (Leonardo of Pisa) was educated in Bugia, now Bejaia in Algeria, a North African port where his father represented merchants from Pisa; there he was taught the Indian numerals.

Fibonacci’s book Liber Abaci, completed in 1202, introduced the Hindu-Arabic place-value numerals to Europe; one section is full of merchants’ problems on prices, profit and converting between currencies.
In Liber Abaci Fibonacci referred to 0 as a sign, while he spoke of the symbols 1 to 9 as numbers; zero was not widely used in Europe for a long time afterwards.
In 1299 the leaders of Florence, a city known for banking and trade, banned the zero and the new numerals and kept to Roman numerals.
A commonly given reason for the Florence ban is fear of fraud: adding a zero on paper easily makes a written amount larger, turning 10 into 100 or 1,000, which Roman numerals did not allow so easily.
Calculating with Roman numerals is slow and clumsy, so over more than 100 years Arabic numerals including zero won out; by the 15th century they were widely accepted.

notes: 批次提示的事件（628 年婆羅摩笈多、1202 年《計算之書》、1299 年佛羅倫斯禁令）都由白名單來源（聖安德魯斯大學 MacTutor、Scientific American、NPR）確認。學界對 1299 年禁令的範圍有不同說法（有研究認為只限銀行帳簿的寫法），出題時把「防偽造」寫成常見的解釋而不是定論。
